products.title: Amazon Frogbit
products.body_html:
Fighting algae or want cover for fry and shrimp? Amazon Frogbit does both at once. Round, spongy leaves sit on the surface while long hair-like roots trail down into the water column — stripping the nitrate algae wants, shading the tank below, and giving shrimplets somewhere to hide.

What You’ll Receive

Fresh, healthy Amazon Frogbit cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®. Choose the pack size that suits your tank:

  • 3 Plants — Starter Pack. For nano tanks under 10 gallons, or anyone who would rather buy a small culture and let it multiply. Frogbit grows fast, so a few plants become a mat within weeks.
  • 6 Plants — Standard Pack. The usual choice for a 10 to 20 gallon tank. Enough to look established from the start without covering the whole surface on day one.
  • 12 Plants — Value / Breeder Pack. For tanks of 40 gallons and up, or breeders who need cover for fry immediately rather than waiting for the plants to spread.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Amazon Frogbit
  • Scientific name — Limnobium laevigatum
  • Also known as — South American Spongeplant, Smooth Frogbit
  • Origin — Central and South America
  • Placement — Floating on the surface
  • Shipped size — 3, 6 or 12 individual plants depending on pack
  • Mature height — Floats; roots trail several inches down
  • Suits — 5 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner. One of the easiest plants you can buy
  • Light — Low to medium is plenty; it sits closest to the light already
  • CO₂ — Not required. It takes carbon straight from the air
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — None. It floats and feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic floater
  • Propagation — Runners; daughter plants appear on their own

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the leaf tops dry. Water sitting on the leaves makes them yellow and rot, so aim filter outflow below the surface and skip the airstone underneath it. This is the single most common way frogbit fails.
  • Leave an air gap under the lid. Condensation dripping back down does exactly the same damage as spray.
  • Buy for where you want to end up, not where you start. Three plants will reach the coverage of twelve in a month or so under decent light. Pay for the larger pack only if you need the shade or the fry cover now.
  • Thin it every week or two. It doubles fast, and a solid mat of frogbit will shade out every plant beneath it — half to two-thirds surface cover is a sensible target.
  • Yellowing leaves usually mean iron or micronutrients, not light. Floating plants feed entirely from the water column and are the first to show a deficiency.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; leaf size and root length vary with lighting and nutrient availability. Not suitable for tanks with strong surface agitation or high flow.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Myriophyllum Mattogrossense
products.body_html:
Myriophyllum mattogrossense is one of the finest-textured background plants available — bright green feathery whorls on slender stems that move with the current. It fills a back wall faster than almost anything else, which is both the appeal and the thing to plan for.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 6 individual, loose-cut stems without root
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 6 stems without root bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 6 stems without root potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mattogrossense Milfoil
  • Scientific name — Myriophyllum mattogrossense
  • Also known as — Green Milfoil, Brazilian Milfoil
  • Origin — Mato Grosso, Brazil
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.0
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil helps, but it feeds mainly from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It feeds from the water, not the substrate. Root tabs do little here. Consistent water column dosing — macros and iron — is what keeps the whorls dense and the green bright.
  • Low light makes it leggy, not dead. Under weak lighting the internodes stretch and the feathering thins out. That is a light problem, not a nutrient one.
  • Fast growth means it shades its neighbors. At eight to sixteen inches and growing quickly, it will overtop anything planted in front of it within weeks. Trim on a schedule rather than when it looks untidy.
  • Handle it gently — the foliage is brittle. Fine whorls shed easily when pulled through water or gravel. Plant stems individually with tweezers rather than pushing a bunch in by hand.
  • Trim and replant the tops. Lower stems go bare as the canopy thickens. Cutting the top few inches and replanting them keeps a background even and doubles your stem count.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Myriophyllum (Milfoil) Care Guide.

Notes

  • Myriophyllum mattogrossense is a fast-growing plant that may require regular trimming to prevent shading other plants. Under low light, stems may become leggy.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Azolla (Fairy Moss)
products.body_html:
Want surface cover that works as a nutrient sponge? Azolla is a floating fern with tiny overlapping leaves that form a soft mat across the water. It shades out algae, strips nitrate fast, and turns red or bronze under strong light or cool weather.

What You’ll Receive

Our Azolla is sold by portion size and packed in resealable bags. The dimensions below refer to the approximate bag size, not the coverage area after the plants are released into your aquarium or pond.

Portion Size Approx. Bag Size Suggested Count Notes
Small 2" × 2" 20+ Great starter portion for nano aquariums and small ponds.
Medium 3" × 3" 80+ Ideal for medium aquariums and water gardens.
Large 4" × 4" 320+ Best value for large aquariums, ponds, and rapid propagation.

Please Note:

  • Plant counts are approximate since Azolla plants naturally vary in size.
  • Azolla is extremely small and reproduces rapidly under suitable growing conditions, so the number of plants will increase over time.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Fairy Moss, Water Fern, Mosquito Fern
  • Scientific name — Azolla caroliniana
  • Placement — Floating
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium to high. Strong light is what turns it red
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 65–85°F · pH 5.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Feeds entirely from the water column
  • Propagation — Fragmentation

Grower’s Notes

  • Keep the surface calm. Azolla will not tolerate strong agitation or spray — water sitting on the fronds rots them. Aim filter outflow below the surface or fence the plants off from the turbulence.
  • Thin it weekly. It doubles quickly and a closed mat shades everything below, including your other plants. Scoop out a third at a time.
  • Red color comes from bright light and cool water, not fertilizer. In a dim warm tank it stays green.
  • It fixes nitrogen through a symbiotic cyanobacterium in its leaves, which is why it grows so fast in water most plants find lean.

Want to go deeper? Read our guide to the Best Floating Plants for Freshwater Aquariums.

Notes

  • Azolla grows rapidly and may require regular thinning in well-lit or nutrient-rich environments. Not recommended for tanks with strong surface agitation or high flow.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.body_html:
Want neon pink rather than red? Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai' holds a genuine hot pink through its narrow elongated leaves, shading to green — a color no other stem plant in our range produces. This listing is the young, miniature size.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pink Chai
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila lancea 'Pink Chai'
  • Also known as — Hygrophila sp. 'Chai', Hygrophila sp. 'Pink Chai', Hygrophila Pink Lady
  • Origin — Natural hybrid of Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia', found at South Island Aquarium in Singapore
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Young miniature plants, roughly 1-3 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light intensifies the pink
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5. Sensitive to sudden changes
  • Substrate — Required. Root and water column feeder

Grower’s Notes

  • Stability matters more than intensity. Pink Chai reacts to sudden shifts in parameters more than most Hygrophila. A steady tank produces better color than a heavily dosed one that swings.
  • Occasional stems revert. The hybrid is stable and cuttings normally come true pink, but a stem may sometimes return to the reddish-brown of the parent Hygrophila lancea 'Araguaia'. That is the hybrid behaving normally, not a mislabeled plant — remove reverted stems if you want the stand to stay uniformly pink.
  • Trim regularly and replant the tops. Topping forces branching, which is what turns a few stems into a block of color.
  • This is the small size. Young plants take time to develop full color — judge it once established rather than on arrival.
  • Also sold at standard size and as sterile Pink Chai Vitro Culture.

products.title: Echinodorus Marble Queen
products.body_html:
Broad leaves marbled in cream and green. Echinodorus 'Marble Queen' is the variegated sword — pattern rather than color, on a plant large enough to hold the middle of a tank. Easier than most variegated aquatics, because the cream is marbling rather than a full loss of chlorophyll.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose bare-root plants, rooted bunched, or rooted potted plants:

  • Loose Bare-Root Plants: Approximately 1–2 loose, bare-root plants for flexible planting.
  • Rooted Bunched: Approximately 1–2 plants, bundled with foam and a plant weight.
  • Rooted Potted: Approximately 1–2 plants, potted in rock wool and a net pot for secure placement.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Marble Queen Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus 'Marble Queen'
  • Also known as — Echinodorus cordifolius 'Marble Queen', Marble Queen Amazon Sword
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the genus is native to the Americas
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner, provided you feed the roots
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — root tabs or aquasoil under the crown.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette; also grows emersed, so it suits paludariums
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on aerial floral stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Variegation is marbling, not albinism. The cream areas sit in a mostly green leaf, so unlike the heavily white Anubias this plant still photosynthesizes normally and stays a beginner plant. What it will do under thin light is revert — push plainer green leaves — rather than decline.
  • Feed it at the roots. Swords take nearly all their nutrition from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone the plant stalls and the pattern washes out, which people misread as a difficult plant rather than a hungry one.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level, never below. Cover the roots and leave the growing point exposed. A buried crown rots from the center.
  • It propagates from floral stalks, not runners. A settled plant sends up a tall stalk carrying plantlets. Leave each attached until it has four or five leaves and its own roots, then cut it free.
  • Expect the first leaves to melt. Grown emersed, so the arriving foliage dies back as it converts. The second flush is the one that shows the marbling properly.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Amazon Sword (Echinodorus) Care Guide.

Notes

Like all Amazon Swords, the Marble Queen may undergo a brief adjustment period after planting. Some leaves may melt back, but healthy roots will quickly sprout new growth once established.

Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Crinum Thaianum
products.body_html:
Want tall, ribbon-like leaves that sway in the current but almost never get eaten? The Onion Plant (Crinum thaianum) grows from a sturdy bulb into long, tough green leaves for the back of a large tank, and it keeps going with very little help.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sprouted Bulb With Leaf | one young bulb with approx. 4+ leaves and minimal roots
  • Potted Sprouted Bulb | one young bulb with approx. 4+ leaves, potted with net pot and rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Onion Plant
  • Scientific name — Crinum thaianum
  • Also known as — Water Onion, Water Onion Plant
  • Origin — Southern Thailand
  • Placement — Background
  • Shipped size — Young bulb with approx. 4+ leaves and minimal roots
  • Mature height — 20–40 in leaves, often longer. In shallower tanks the leaves reach the surface and lie along it
  • Suits — 30 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Slow while it settles in

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — True aquatic
  • Propagation — Daughter bulbs that form beside the parent

Grower’s Notes

  • Plant the roots, not the whole bulb. Bury the roots and the base, and keep at least the top half of the bulb above the gravel. A fully buried bulb can rot.
  • It arrives with only a few roots. That is normal for a bulb plant. A root tab under it helps new roots grow, and the bulb's stored energy carries it while they do.
  • Expect a slow start. New leaves come one at a time at first, then faster once the roots take hold. Leave it in one spot.
  • The leaves are thick and tough, so most fish that nibble soft plants leave it alone.
  • Long leaves can shade plants beneath them. Trim old or damaged leaves at the base, and give it the back corner of the tank.

products.body_html:
Like the soft, needle-leaf look of Mayaca fluviatilis but want more depth? Mayaca sellowiana (often sold as Mayaca sellowiniana) grows the same fine, feathery stems in a darker, richer green, so a stand of it reads as a solid block of color instead of a light haze.

Plant Profile

  • Scientific name — Mayaca sellowiana
  • Also known as — Mayaca Sellowiniana, Mayaca sellowiniana
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground to background

  • Mature height — 6–14 in

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Stronger light keeps the stems compact and the color deep
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required

  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings. Trim and replant the stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Treat it like Mayaca fluviatilis, and expect a darker green. The two share the same fine needle leaves and the same needs. Plant them side by side and the light and dark greens make each other stand out.

  • Plant stems one at a time, about an inch apart. Fine-leaved stems packed in a bunch shade each other and drop their lower leaves.
  • Handle the stems at the base. The fine leaves strip off where you pinch, and bare spots don't grow back.
  • The dark, fine texture sets off red and broad-leaved plants such as Ludwigia and Alternanthera, and gives shrimp and small fish good cover.

products.body_html:

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient-rich soil or root tabs

Grower's Notes

  • Light decides whether it is yellow or just green. Under medium light the leaves lean pale green; stronger light brings out the golden tone and the orange-red edging. This is the one variable worth adjusting if the color disappoints.
  • Root tabs are not optional. Swords take almost everything from the substrate. In inert gravel with liquid dosing alone the yellow washes out to a sickly pale green, which is easy to mistake for a deficiency in the water column.
  • Never bury the crown. Cover the roots and leave the growing point at substrate level. A buried crown rots from the center and does not recover.
  • It propagates from flower stalks, not runners. A mature plant sends up an inflorescence carrying plantlets along its length; let each root and grow three or four leaves before separating it.
  • Use it against green, not against red. Yellow-green next to red plants muddies both. Set against dark green foliage or wood it does what it is bought for.

products.title: Hydrotriche Hottoniiflora
products.body_html:
Hydrotriche hottoniiflora is an aquatic plant species that belongs to the family Hydrocharitaceae. It is commonly known as the feathered water sprite or the water nymph.

This plant is native to tropical Africa and is widely distributed throughout the continent. It is a popular aquarium plant due to its delicate, feathery leaves that add an elegant touch to any aquascape. Hydrotriche hottoniiflora is also known for its fast growth rate, making it an excellent choice for beginners who want to quickly fill in their aquarium with lush vegetation.

In addition to its aesthetic appeal, Hydrotriche hottoniiflora is also a beneficial plant for the aquarium ecosystem. It helps to oxygenate the water, absorb excess nutrients, and provide hiding places for fish and invertebrates.

To successfully grow Hydrotriche hottoniiflora in an aquarium, it requires moderate to high lighting and nutrient-rich water. It can be propagated by cutting the stem and replanting it, and it is relatively easy to care for.

Overall, Hydrotriche hottoniiflora is an excellent choice for aquarists looking to add a touch of elegance and benefit the ecosystem of their aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mattogrossense Milfoil
  • Scientific name — Myriophyllum mattogrossense
  • Also known as — Myrio, Green Mosaic Plant, Mattogrossense Watermilfoil, Matogrosso milfoil
  • Origin — Mato Grosso, Brazil
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.0
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil helps, but it feeds mainly from the water column

Grower's Notes

  • It feeds from the water, not the substrate. Root tabs do little here. Consistent water column dosing — macros and iron — is what keeps the whorls dense and the green bright.
  • Separate the plantlets before planting. Rinse the gel off completely and plant small groups of two or three stems an inch apart. Planted as one lump the center rots before it roots.
  • Low light makes it leggy, not dead. Under weak lighting the internodes stretch and the feathering thins out. That is a light problem, not a nutrient one.
  • Handle it gently — the foliage is brittle. Fine whorls shed easily when pulled through water or gravel. Use tweezers rather than pushing stems in by hand.
  • Trim on a schedule. At eight to sixteen inches and growing fast, it will overtop anything planted in front of it within weeks. Cut the tops and replant them to keep the group even.

products.body_html:
Java Moss is the plant people start with and never remove. It attaches to anything, grows in almost any light, and needs no substrate or CO₂ — and the tangle of fine shoots is where shrimp graze and fry hide. This is the tissue culture version, so it arrives without the snails and algae that hitch a ride on portion-grown moss.

What You'll Receive

  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Java Moss
  • Scientific name — Taxiphyllum barbieri
  • Also known as — long sold under the misapplied name Vesicularia dubyana
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground; attaches to driftwood, stone, or decor

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner

Grower's Notes

  • Spread it thin when you attach it. A thick pad of moss suffocates its own base — the underside browns and detaches, taking the whole mat with it. A single layer tied over wood or mesh grows into a far denser result.
  • Cooler water keeps it tidy. Java Moss is happiest below the high end of its range. Above about 80°F the shoots stretch, thin out and trap more detritus.
  • Trim it to make it thicker. Cutting the surface with scissors forces branching from lower down. An untrimmed clump grows long and stringy instead of compact.
  • Keep flow across it. Moss in dead water collects debris, and debris is what algae grows on. Moderate current keeps it clean without needing to be manhandled.
  • Tissue culture moss starts small. The bag holds fine, pale shoots rather than a ready-made mat. Spread the portion over your hardscape and give it a month or two — it thickens considerably as it converts to submersed growth.

products.title: Cyperus Helferi Vitro Culture
products.body_html:

Cyperus helferi grows long ribbon-like blades from a central rosette, giving the swaying grass effect of a Vallisneria without the running — it is a true sedge, so it thickens in place instead of colonizing the tank.   • 10 Bags: Ten 4-inch Vitro Culture® bags containing many small plantlets per bag, ideal for large aquariums, propagation, or aquascape layouts.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Helfer's Cyperus
  • Scientific name — Cyperus helferi
  • Also known as — Aquarium Umbrella Grass
  • Origin — Thailand and Myanmar
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — 4-inch bag of small plantlets
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium. Stronger light keeps growth dense and upright
  • CO₂ — Not required, though it produces longer blades with it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5

  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Grows well emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Side shoots from the base; separate once they have their own roots

Grower's Notes

  • It clumps rather than spreads. Vallisneria runs across the substrate and colonizes wherever it lands; Cyperus stays put and thickens from the base. That makes it far easier to control in a designed layout — and the reason to choose it if Vallisneria has taken over a tank on you before.
  • Plant it where there is flow. The long flexible blades move with current, and that motion is most of what you are buying. In a dead corner it just stands still.
  • Feed at the roots. It is a strong root feeder and grows short and pale in inert gravel.
  • Rinse the gel off and separate the plantlets before planting, spacing them out so each rosette has room to widen.
  • Tissue culture stock arrives small. Give it a few months to build the long blades — this is not an instant background.

products.body_html:
Bright yellow-green leaves in a genus that is otherwise uniformly dark. Anubias Golden holds a golden-lime tone that reads as a highlight against wood, stone and the deep green of everything else in the tank — with the same undemanding rhizome as any other Anubias. This is the sterile tissue-culture format.

What You'll Receive

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Golden Anubias
  • Scientific name — Anubias barteri var. 'Golden'
  • Also known as — Anubias Golden Nana
  • Origin — Cultivated variety; the genus is native to West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 4-6 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Shade suits it; strong light means algae on slow-turning leaves.
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or stone.

Grower's Notes

  • The gold is new growth, not variegation. Each leaf emerges pale golden-lime and darkens toward green as it matures, so the color sits at the growing tip rather than being fixed in the leaf. That also means it is normally pigmented — no harder to grow than any other Anubias.
  • Place it against something dark. The pale new growth is what you are paying for, and it disappears against light sand or pale stone. Dark wood or black lava rock is where it earns its price.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots can go into substrate; the rhizome cannot. Buried, it rots — the most common way an Anubias is lost.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the clumps before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Keep it shaded. Growth is slow enough that algae settles on a leaf faster than the plant replaces it.

Rotala rotundifolia 'Green' is the plant to reach for when you want the shape of a Rotala hedge without the demands that come with the red forms. Round green leaves, fast upright growth, and no CO₂ requirement — it fills the back of a low-tech tank faster than almost anything else in the catalog.

  • Also known as — Rotala indica 'Green', Rotala sp. 'Green', Green Compact
  • Origin — Southeast Asia

Care

products.body_html:
Marsilea hirsuta is a fern that spends its life pretending to be clover. It spreads by runners across the substrate, throwing up single, double, and four-lobed leaves depending on conditions — and unlike most carpets it will do this without pressurized CO₂, just slowly.

What You'll Receive

  • Origin — Australia
  • Placement — Foreground

  • Give it substrate depth. Twelve to twenty inches of leaf needs a deep, well-fed root run. Two inches of nutrient substrate minimum, or root tabs pushed under each crown.
  • Crypt melt is expected and is not failure. Tissue culture plantlets shed their emersed leaves as they convert to submersed growth. Leave the roots undisturbed — new leaves come from the crown within three to six weeks.
  • Plant the crown at substrate level. Bury the roots and leave the growing point exposed. A buried crown rots from the center.
  • Compare it with our other tall crypts. Balansae is the same species with wider, hammered leaves; Retrospiralis is shorter and more reddish. All three do the same job at the back of a low-tech tank.

products.title: Dwarf Sagittaria Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want a grass carpet without CO₂? Sagittaria subulata is the plant that gets most people there. It spreads by runners on its own, tolerates low light, and — unusually — changes height with your lighting: short and tight under bright light, taller and more ribbon-like in shade. That makes one plant do foreground or midground work depending where you put it. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag or 2.5-inch cup containing healthy Sagittaria subulata plantlets—carefully grown, ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Dwarf Sagittaria
  • Scientific name — Sagittaria subulata
  • Also known as — Dwarf Sag, Awl-leaf arrowhead
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 4–8 in, shorter under strong light
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Brighter light keeps it low and compact
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Light controls height, not growth. If your Sag is running tall and floppy, it isn't sick — it's reaching. More light brings it down. This is the single most useful thing to know about the plant.
  • It feeds at the roots. Without a nutrient substrate or root tabs, runners slow and new plantlets stay small.
  • Runners travel where they like. Trim stray runners at the substrate to keep the carpet inside its boundary.
  • Expect a pause after planting. Tissue-culture plantlets convert from emersed to submerged form over two to three weeks before they start running.
  • Plant the plantlets in small clumps an inch apart rather than one big mass — they fill the gaps themselves and root faster in small groups.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Dwarf Sagittaria Care Guide.

products.title: Vallisneria Spiralis (Jungle Val)
products.body_html:
Ribbon-like leaves that reach the surface and trail along it, moving with the flow. Jungle Val is the classic background curtain — fast, undemanding, and one of the few plants that fills a tall tank without CO₂ or strong lighting.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Jungle Val, Straight Vallisneria, Italian Eelgrass
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria spiralis
  • Origin — Southern Europe, Africa and Asia
  • Placement — Background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 2-3 bare-root plants, roughly 6-12 in
  • Mature height — 20–36 in
  • Suits — 30 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots, and this is the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • It feeds at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads — root tabs are what turn three plants into a curtain.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way. Remove whole leaves at the base instead.
  • It tolerates hard, alkaline water better than almost any other background plant, which is why it works in tanks where stems struggle.
  • Too tall for your tank? At 20-36 inches this needs real depth. Corkscrew Val stays 8-12 in and Vallisneria torta only 4-8 in.

products.title: Ammannia Senegalensis
products.body_html:
Copper and orange, not just red. Ammannia senegalensis runs through a wider color range than most red stems — fiery red through copper into orange, on narrow pointed leaves that curl slightly at the edges. Native to West Africa, and one of the faster-growing red plants once it settles.

Care

products.title: Micro Sword
products.body_html:
Want a grass carpet rather than a leafy one? Micro Sword spreads by runner into a fine, low meadow of narrow blades — the closest thing in the hobby to a lawn. It is slower and more demanding than it looks, and it rewards a nutrient substrate more than almost any other carpet.

What You’ll Receive

Choose from our selection of nursery-grown Lilaeopsis brasiliensis:

  • Loose Bare Root Plants: Approximately a small clump bare root portion
  • Bunched Plants: Small clump bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Potted in a net pot with rock wool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Micro Sword, Brazilian Micro Sword
  • Scientific name — Lilaeopsis brasiliensis
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Foreground
  • Shipped size — Small bare-root clump portion
  • Mature height — 1–3 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Light reaching the substrate is what makes it carpet rather than stretch
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required. It carpets faster and denser with it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • Separate the portion into small clumps and plant them an inch apart. Planted as one mass it takes far longer to spread, because runners only travel into open substrate.
  • Root tabs decide the outcome. In inert gravel Micro Sword survives but never thickens — this is the most common reason a carpet stalls.
  • It is slow to start. Expect little visible progress for the first month while it roots, then steady spread. Do not replant it because nothing is happening.
  • Some melt after planting is normal; new submersed blades come from the runners rather than the original leaves.

Despite the name, this is not a sword plant. Lilaeopsis is unrelated to Echinodorus (Amazon Swords) or Helanthium (chain swords) — it stays small and carpets, where true swords grow large or spread as rosettes.

Finer blades for a nano tank? See Micro Sword Narrow Leaf.

products.title: Cryptocoryne Lutea Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
An earthy Crypt that stays small. Cryptocoryne lutea grows narrow, slightly wavy leaves in olive-green to brown on a compact upright rosette — muted, natural tones that sit well against driftwood and stone rather than competing with them. Native to Sri Lanka and one of the more reliable species in the genus. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You’ll Receive

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Crypt Lutea
  • Scientific name — Cryptocoryne lutea
  • Origin — Sri Lanka
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 2–4 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Intense light is not needed
  • CO₂ — Not required

  • Place it once. Every move triggers another melt.

Floating oval leaves on long stems, from a bulb. Aponogeton natans is the surface-leaved member of the genus — it sends leaves up on long petioles to lie flat on the water rather than standing submerged, giving a lily-like effect without a lily's spread. Native to Sri Lanka and India.

products.title: Bucephalandra Godzilla Green Bonsai Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Godzilla Green Bonsai has unusually small, textured dark green leaves on a plant that reaches three to five inches — the leaf-to-plant ratio is what gives it the bonsai look, dense foliage on a structure that reads as miniature rather than merely small. This is the tissue-culture format.

What You'll Receive

  • One sealed 4-inch Vitro Culture® tissue culture bag
  • Approximately 4 small plantlets grown in sterile nutrient gel
  • 100% free from snails, algae, pesticides and pathogens
  • Rinse the gel away and separate the plantlets before planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Godzilla Green Bonsai Buce
  • Scientific name — Bucephalandra sp. 'Godzilla Green Bonsai'
  • Also known as — Buce Godzilla Green, Mini Buce Bonsai
  • Origin — Borneo (genus range)
  • Placement — Midground, attached to hardscape
  • Mature height — 3-5 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium. Too much light brings algae the plant is too slow to outgrow.
  • CO₂ — Not required. Deepens color and speeds growth if you already run it.
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — None needed. Epiphyte; attaches to wood or rock.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rhizome creeper; grows submersed or emersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • This one improves with age, which most plants do not. Small leaves accumulating on a thickening rhizome over years is exactly what produces the bonsai character. Plant it somewhere you will not want to move it.
  • Rinse the gel off completely and separate the four plantlets before attaching. Leftover nutrient agar clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or rock and leave it exposed; buried rhizomes rot.
  • Farm-raised, not wild-collected. All the Bucephalandra we carry is farm-grown, and much of it is raised from tissue culture rather than collected from Borneo.
  • Gentle to moderate flow suits it — enough to keep debris off the small leaves, not enough to lift a young rhizome off its mount before the roots grip.

products.title: Nymphaea Tina | Violet Tropical Water Lily
products.body_html:
Nymphaea 'Tina' is a tropical day-bloomer that does something most lilies do not — it grows new plants on its own leaves. Deep violet-purple cup-shaped flowers with golden centers, a genuine sweet scent, and pads that emerge bronze before turning green.

What You'll Receive

You will receive 1 young, freshly harvested waterlily tuber.

  • All tubers/rhizomes are carefully inspected before shipping and guaranteed viable, healthy, and ready to grow in a proper pond environment.
  • Note: The images shown are sample representations. The actual product you receive may not be identical, as live plants vary in size and stage.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Tina Tropical Water Lily
  • Scientific name — Nymphaea 'Tina'
  • Type — Tropical, day-blooming, viviparous
  • Flower — Cup-shaped violet-purple with golden-yellow centers, lightly fragrant
  • Origin — Cultivated hybrid
  • Placement — Centerpiece in a pond or container water garden; also tanks 20 gallons and up
  • Mature height — 12-24 inches
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Sunlight — Full sun, 6+ hours daily
  • Planting depth — 12-24 inches from soil surface to water surface
  • Water — 72-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Soil — Heavy clay or loam, capped with gravel; this is a root feeder
  • Feeding — Aquatic fertilizer tablets monthly through the growing season
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower's Notes

  • It also propagates off its own pads. Beyond dividing the rhizome, this viviparous cultivar grows a small plantlet at the center of a mature leaf. Let it develop roots and two or three leaves of its own, then cut the pad free and pot it — one tuber becomes several plants in a season.
  • Tropical means it will not overwinter outdoors in a cold region. The tuber has to be lifted and stored in moist conditions over winter unless you are in a warm climate. Hardy lilies stay in the pond; this one does not.
  • Six hours of direct sun is the requirement. Shade is the usual reason a lily makes plenty of pads and few flowers.
  • Indoors, expect pads before flowers. A pond or container water garden is where most 'Tina' go, but it will live in a tank of 20 gallons or larger. Blooming there takes light as strong as sun over a long daily run; anything dimmer or shorter gives leaves only. It grows fast, so trim the pads often or they close over the surface.
  • Plant the tuber with the crown clear of the soil. Set it upright with the growing tip above the soil line, then cap with gravel. Buried crowns rot.
  • The flowers stand above the water. Unlike hardy lilies, which float their blooms, tropicals hold theirs on stems clear of the surface — which is why the scent actually reaches you.

Planting Instructions for Water Lily

There are two main types of water lilies, tropical and hardy. The differences between tropical and hardy water lilies are a growing habit. Tropical water lilies don't do well in winter. Hardy water lilies, on the other hand, can tolerate the cold. Tropical water lilies tubers must be removed from the pond and stored in moist conditions to come back in the future years. In warm climates, they can remain in the pond.

Notes

  • All water lilies are shipped bare-root (as tubers) and should be planted immediately upon arrival for best results. Bloom and leaf color, size, and shape may vary slightly depending on lighting, water quality, and plant maturity.

products.title: Microsorum Pteropus Windelov Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Leaf tips that branch and re-branch into fine crests instead of ending in a point. Leptochilus pteropus 'Windelov' — the Lace Java Fern — is the cultivar that gives a low-tech tank fine detail without needing CO₂ or bright light. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing multiple healthy plantlets:

  • Approximately 6+ leaves total
  • May arrive as individual leaves or small plantlets, not fully connected
  • Each plantlet includes developing roots for easy attachment and growth

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Lace Java Fern
  • Scientific name — Leptochilus pteropus 'Windelov' (syn. Microsorum pteropus)
  • Origin — Cultivated form; the species is native to Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground, attached to driftwood, stone or décor
  • Mature height — 4-8 inches
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Epiphyte — attach the rhizome to hardscape and never bury it.
  • Growth habit — Amphibious; grows emersed as well as submersed
  • Propagation — Rhizome division, plus plantlets from mature leaves

Grower's Notes

  • Rinse the gel off, and expect loose pieces. Tissue-culture Windelov often separates into individual leaves rather than a single clump. That is normal — each piece with a scrap of rhizome and a root will grow. Rinse until the roots feel clean, then attach the pieces close together.
  • Expect some melt. Leaves may die back as the plant converts from lab conditions to submerged growth. As long as the rhizome stays firm and green, new growth follows.
  • Never bury the rhizome. Roots may go into substrate; the green horizontal stem must stay in open water or it rots — the single most common way a Java Fern is killed.
  • Keep the light modest. Java Fern grows too slowly to outgrow algae, and algae caught in a finely branched leaf tip is close to impossible to clean out. Shade is the defense.
  • Sterile media is the point. No snails, no algae spores, no pesticide residue — which is what makes this format the right choice for a shrimp tank.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Java Fern Care Guide.

Notes

  • Tissue culture plants are grown in sterile gel and may require rinsing before planting.
  • Leaves may melt slightly during transition as the plant adapts to submerged conditions—this is normal.
  • Proper acclimation will ensure healthy new growth.

products.title: Echinodorus Gabrielii
products.body_html:
Echinodorus gabrielii is a medium-sized sword — narrow, upright leaves in fresh green that stay tidier than the broad-leaved Amazon types without being a small plant. Planted as a group it reads as a soft green screen; planted alone in a mid-sized tank it works as the centerpiece.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Bare-root Plants, Bunch Plants or Potted Plants
  • Bare-root Plants | loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunch Plants | rooted plants bundle with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants | rooted plants potted with net pot and rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Gabrielii Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus gabrielii
  • Also known as — Gabriel's Sword
  • Origin — South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 10-16 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.5-7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — nutrient-rich soil or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious rosette
  • Propagation — Adventitious plantlets on flower stalks

Grower's Notes

  • Plan for a medium sword, not a small one. At 10 to 16 inches it needs a tank with height — 20 gallons upward. It is tidier than an Amazon Sword because the leaves are narrower, not because the plant is smaller.
  • Root tabs are not optional. Like every Echinodorus this is a heavy root feeder — it builds a large root mass and takes almost everything from the substrate. Liquid dosing alone gives small pale leaves no matter how good the lighting is.
  • Never bury the crown. Cover the roots and leave the growing point at substrate level. A buried crown rots from the center and does not recover.
  • Narrow leaves change how you use it. Broad-leaved swords shade everything around them. Gabrielii's slimmer upright foliage lets light through, so it can sit closer to other plants without smothering them.
  • Expect the first leaves to melt as it converts from emersed nursery growth. The second flush is the submerged form — judge the plant on that.

products.title: Hygrophila Pinnatifida Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Hygrophila pinnatifida grows sideways. Deeply lobed, fern-like leaves in olive and bronze sit on stems that creep across hardscape and root into it — the only Hygrophila that will attach to wood and stone rather than standing upright in substrate.

What You'll Receive

  • 1 portion of Hygrophila pinnatifida in Vitro Culture sealed 4-inch bag
  • Healthy, young plantlets grown in nutrient gel—ready to rinse and plant

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pinnatifida
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila pinnatifida
  • Also known as — Indian Hygrophila
  • Origin — Western Ghats, India
  • Placement — Midground; attaches to driftwood and stone
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 inches
  • Mature height — 4-10 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.5
  • Substrate — Not required if attached to hardscape; nutrient substrate if planted
  • Growth habit — Amphibious creeping stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • Pinholes in the leaves mean potassium. Pinnatifida is the plant in most tanks that shows a potassium shortfall first — small holes appear in older leaves and spread. Dosing potassium clears it within a few weeks; it is not a pest or a disease.
  • Tie it to wood, do not plant it deep. Attached to hardscape it sends roots down into the surface and creeps outward, which is how it is meant to be used. Buried too deep in substrate the lower stem rots.
  • Trimming decides the shape. Left alone it runs horizontally along its support. Topped repeatedly it bushes upward instead. Both look good — decide which you want before it settles in.
  • Bronze and red need light on the tops. Under low light it stays olive green. The reddish tone develops on leaves closest to the surface, so position it where it is not shaded by taller plants.
  • Want more red? The 'UK' collection from Uttara Kannada reddens more readily than this standard form under the same conditions.

products.title: Weeping Moss Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
The moss that grows downward. Vesicularia ferriei — Weeping Moss — sends its fronds hanging rather than spreading, so attached to a branch tip it forms a cascade instead of a mat. That habit is why it is the standard choice for waterfall effects and moss trees. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Weeping Moss
  • Scientific name — Vesicularia ferriei
  • Type — Rheophyte / epiphyte

Care

products.title: Guppy Grass
products.body_html:
The plant breeders buy by the handful. Najas guadalupensis — Guppy Grass — grows fast in almost any conditions, needs no substrate, and forms a dense tangle that newborn fry and shrimplets disappear into. It also strips nitrate out of the water faster than most plants, which is why breeding tanks and fry tanks run cleaner with it in them.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as loose Fresh-cut plants, Bunched plants, or Potted plants
  • Fresh-cut plants | Approx. 6 stems, loose fresh-cut stems without root
  • Bunched plants | Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants | Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems without root, potted with net pot and rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Guppy Grass
  • Scientific name — Najas guadalupensis
  • Also known as — Najas Grass, Common Water Nymph
  • Origin — North and Central America
  • Placement — Midground, background, or left floating
  • Mature height — 6–20 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 65–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5. Tolerates cooler water than most tropical plants
  • Substrate — Not required. Grows planted or floating
  • Growth habit — True aquatic. Does not grow emersed
  • Propagation — Fragmentation — broken pieces keep growing

Grower’s Notes

  • Float it in a breeding tank and forget it. No substrate, no planting, no CO₂ — a floating mass gives fry immediate cover and starts pulling nitrate down from day one. That combination is why it outsells prettier plants among breeders.
  • It is brittle by design. Stems snap and every fragment keeps growing — that's the propagation method, but it also means it spreads unless you net out loose pieces at water changes.
  • Fast growth is the algae control. In a new tank, Guppy Grass takes up the nutrients algae would otherwise use.
  • It tolerates cool water down to 65°F, so it works in unheated and lightly heated tanks where tropical stems struggle.
  • Trim hard and often. Left alone it will fill the tank and shade everything underneath.

  • Runners travel fast. Pull unwanted plantlets by hand rather than cutting, and expect to thin it every month or two.
  • Sand or soil suits it better than coarse gravel, which the runners struggle to travel through.

products.title: Vallisneria Americana
products.body_html:
Want Vallisneria that won't take over the tank? Corkscrew Val stays 8 to 12 inches instead of running to the surface, and twists its blades along their whole length into tight spirals. Of our three twisted Vals, this is the one with the widest blade — the spirals read boldly rather than as fine threads.

  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Corkscrew Val, also known as Twisted Val
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria americana 'Asiatica'
  • Origin — Asia (this cultivar); the species is North American
  • Placement — Midground, or foreground in a large tank
  • Shipped size — Approx. 2-3 bare-root plants, roughly 4-8 in

  • Difficulty — Beginner

  • Wide blades, mid height. Jungle Val and spiralis keep growing until they hit the surface and trail along it. 'Asiatica' tops out around a foot, which is why it works where taller Vallisneria would swamp the layout.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a colony.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way. Remove whole leaves at the base instead.
  • Runners travel fast. Pull unwanted plantlets by hand rather than cutting, and expect to thin it every month or two once established.

Choosing between our twisted Vallisneria

  • Vallisneria torta — shortest, 4–8 in. Foreground, midground and nano tanks.
  • Vallisneria americana 'Asiatica' (this plant) — 8–12 in, with a wider twisted blade.
  • Vallisneria 'Contortionist' — 10–20 in, with a narrower twisted blade. Background.

products.title: Rotala Mini Butterfly
products.body_html:
Rotala Mini Butterfly stays short where most Rotala runs tall. Tiny paired leaves sit tight along the stem, and under strong light the growing tips shift from green through peach into pink. At three to six inches it works as a colored patch in the front half of a tank rather than a background hedge.

What You'll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 6 individual, loose-cut stems without root
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 6 stems without root, bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 6 stems without root, potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Butterfly
  • Scientific name — Rotala sp. 'Mini Butterfly'
  • Also known as — Rotala Butterfly
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Foreground to midground
  • Mature height — 3-6 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.0
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It arrives green and colors up in your tank. Nursery stock is grown for health, not color. Pink and red develop over several weeks once the plant is under your own lighting, so judge it on the third set of leaves rather than the first.
  • Plant stems individually, not as a bunch. Remove the foam and weight and push each stem into the substrate about half an inch apart. Bundled stems rot where the wrap sits and the center of the group thins out.
  • Trim it low and often. Cutting the tops repeatedly is what keeps this variety short and dense. Left untrimmed it stretches and loses the compact form it is bought for.
  • Lean nitrate deepens the pink. Keeping nitrate modest while dosing iron and micros consistently is what shifts the tips from green to pink. Cutting nutrients off entirely stalls the plant instead.
  • Give it front-row light. At three to six inches it sits low, so anything planted in front of it will shade it out and the color goes with the light.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Rotala Care Guide.

Notes

  • Rotala Mini Butterfly may arrive green when shipped. With proper lighting, CO₂, and nutrients, the pink and red coloration will emerge over time.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Vallisneria nana 'Striped'
products.body_html:
Want pattern on a narrow-leaved Val? Vallisneria nana 'Striped' — also sold as Tiger Val — carries brown striping and speckling along slim green blades. It gives you markings and movement without the solid curtain a broad-leaved Vallisneria creates.

Sold as loose bare-root plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Bare-root Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual loose, bare-root plants
  • Bunched Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants bundled with foam and a plant weight
  • Potted Plants: Approximately 2–3 individual bare-root plants potted in rockwool and net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Striped Vallisneria Nana, also known as Tiger Vallisneria
  • Scientific name — Vallisneria nana 'Striped'
  • Also known as — Vallisneria nana 'Tiger'
  • Placement — Background
  • Mature height — 20–30 in
  • Leaf width — Narrow, though noticeably wider than standard nana
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Low to medium
  • CO₂ — Not required
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.5–8.0. Tolerates hard, alkaline water well
  • Substrate — Required. Root feeder — nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Fully aquatic
  • Propagation — Substrate runners

Grower’s Notes

  • It stays green under strong light. This is the practical difference from Vallisneria spiralis 'Leopard', which develops red tones and heavier marbling under intensity. Striped keeps its green base with brown tiger markings whatever you throw at it.
  • Striping varies plant to plant, and some leaves carry more than others. That is normal for this cultivar rather than a sign of a poor specimen.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots — the usual reason a new Val fails in the first fortnight.
  • Feed at the roots. In inert gravel it survives but barely spreads; root tabs are what turn three plants into a stand.
  • Don't trim the tops to control height. Cut Val leaves brown at the cut and stay that way — remove whole leaves at the base instead.

Want the finest blade instead? Standard Vallisneria nana is the narrowest in the genus at roughly 1 mm, without the markings.

products.title: Ludwigia Pantanal
products.body_html:
One of the most vividly colored stem plants in the hobby, and one of the least tolerant. Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Pantanal' carries fine whorled leaves that run deep red into fiery orange — but only under strong light, CO₂ and steady feeding. From the Pantanal wetlands of South America. Grown emersed at our nursery.

What You'll Receive

Choose the format that suits your aquascaping needs:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 6+ unrooted stems
  • Bunched Plants: 6+ fresh-cut stems without root bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: 6+ fresh-cut stems potted in rockwool within a 2-inch net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Pantanal
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia sp. 'Pantanal'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Pantanal'
  • Origin — Pantanal wetlands, South America
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6+ fresh-cut stems, no roots
  • Mature height — 6–14 in
  • Suits — 20 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. High light is what produces the color
  • CO₂ — Recommended, in practice near-essential for color
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft, low-carbonate water
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Green emersed, red submerged
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower's Notes

  • It ships green and that is correct. Our nursery stock is emersed, with upright green stems and plain leaves. The red and orange appear only after several weeks of submerged growth under strong light — nothing has gone wrong in the first fortnight.
  • Soft water is not optional. Pantanal wants low carbonate hardness. In hard alkaline tap water it stunts at the tips whatever else you do — test KH rather than chasing a pH number.
  • This is the most demanding Ludwigia we sell. It reacts to swings in CO₂, photoperiod or dosing faster than almost any other stem plant, usually by dropping its lower leaves. Have the tank running steadily first.
  • Trim the tops and replant them — cuttings color faster than the stumps regrow. Fine whorled leaves contrast strongly against broad-leaved plants, so use it where that difference shows.
  • Also available as sterile Ludwigia Pantanal Vitro Culture for a pest-free start.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Ludwigia Pantanal requires high light, pressurized CO₂, and stable nutrient dosing to achieve its vibrant coloration and healthy growth. It is not suitable for low-tech setups. Emersed plants will arrive green and may undergo a transitional phase with some leaf melt before adapting to submerged growth.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Senegalensis Guinea Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Veins you can actually see. Ludwigia senegalensis runs a network of dark red veins across brick-red to orange leaves — pattern rather than a flat block of color, and unlike anything else in the genus. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format, which matters for a plant this sensitive to a rough start.

What You'll Receive

  • Sold as a Tissue Culture Plants with vitamin liquid/gel
  • Bag size: Approx. 4 inches. Yield many small plants
  • Tissue Culture Technology | 100% Free from Snail, Algae, Pathogen, and Bacteria plus Extended Shelf Life on all in Vitro Plants

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Senegalensis
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia senegalensis
  • Also known as — Ludwigia sp. 'Guinea', Guinea Ludwigia
  • Origin — West Africa
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — Medium to high. The vein pattern and brick-red color both depend on it
  • CO₂ — Recommended. In practice this plant rarely performs without it
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient-rich substrate plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim side shoots and replant

Grower's Notes

  • Stability is the requirement, not any single value. Senegalensis punishes swings in CO₂, temperature and dosing more than it punishes any particular parameter being slightly off. A settled, mature tank suits it; a new one usually does not.
  • Starting from plantlets is an advantage with this species. Cultured stock has no established growth habit to unlearn, so it adapts to your water rather than reacting to the change.
  • The veining is what you are paying for, and it needs light to show. Under weak lighting the leaves stay plain green and the pattern disappears.
  • Plant the plantlets separately with space between them. Crowded, the lower leaves shade out and the pattern is lost exactly where you would see it.
  • Frequently confused with Ludwigia glandulosa. They look similar but come from opposite sides of the Atlantic — glandulosa is North American, this is West African.

products.title: Rotala Macrandra Mini Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
Want macrandra color in a plant that stays under 10 inches? Rotala macrandra 'Mini' carries the same pink-to-red coloring as the full-size plant on leaves a fraction of the size. This is the sterile tissue culture (Vitro Culture) format: young plantlets that adapt to your water more readily than mature cut stems.

What You'll Receive

One 4-inch sealed Vitro Culture® bag containing healthy Rotala macrandra 'Mini' plantlets—ready to rinse, acclimate, and plant in your aquarium.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Mini Macrandra
  • Scientific name — Rotala macrandra 'Mini'
  • Also known as — Rotala Macrandra Mini Red
  • Origin — India (species range); this form is aquarium-developed
  • Placement — Midground
  • Shipped size — Small tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 inches
  • Mature height — 4-10 inches
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Under medium light it stays green-pink and stretches
  • CO₂ — Recommended. In practice, high light without injection produces algae rather than red leaves
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Soft water gives the best color
  • Substrate — Required. Rich nutrient substrate plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Compact stems with small leaves, longish-ovoid with upturned margins or roundish-ovoid
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • This is the hardest Rotala in common cultivation, scaled down. Small leaves do not mean an easier plant: mini macrandra wants the same CO₂, rich substrate and strong light as the full-size form, with less margin for error.
  • Color is a light-and-iron response. Under strong light with iron dosing and lean nitrate it comes through properly red.
  • Rinse the gel off completely with aquarium or dechlorinated water and separate the plantlets before planting. Tissue culture gel left in the tank clouds water and feeds algae.
  • Plant the plantlets individually, about an inch apart. Crowded groups shade their own lower leaves and go bare from the base.
  • Expect some melting during the switch from tissue culture to submerged growth. Judge the plant by its new leaves, not the ones it arrived with.

Prefer fresh-cut stems? See Rotala Macrandra Mini.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference. Actual plant color and form may vary based on lighting, nutrients, and aquarium conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Cabomba furcata 'Super Magenta'
products.body_html:
Chasing a color no other aquarium plant produces? Cabomba Super Magenta holds a true violet — deep purple and neon magenta on fine fan-shaped whorls. It is the most demanding plant we sell, and it is the only one that color exists in.

What You’ll Receive

  • Fresh, healthy Cabomba Super Magenta cultivated and prepared by Aquarium Plants Factory®, available in convenient planting formats:
  • Fresh Cut Plants: Approximately 6 loose, fresh-cut stems without roots
  • Fresh Cut Bunched: Approximately 6 stems bundled with foam and a plant weight for easy placement
  • Fresh Cut Potted: About 6 stems potted securely in a net pot with rockwool for stability and easy planting

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Super Magenta Cabomba
  • Scientific name — Cabomba furcata 'Super Magenta'
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Growth rate — Fast

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced. This one genuinely is
  • Light — High, and non-negotiable
  • CO₂ — Required. Pressurized, not liquid carbon
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–6.8, soft and acidic
  • Feeding — Water column; iron drives the magenta
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower’s Notes

  • Soft acidic water is the make-or-break condition. Above pH 7 it declines no matter how good your light and CO₂ are — more Cabomba furcata is lost to hard water than to anything else.
  • Stability matters more than richness. It sheds whole whorls after a water change that swings temperature or chemistry sharply, so keep changes small and consistent.
  • Plant the stems individually, an inch or so apart. Bunched together they shade each other and rot from the middle out.
  • It will not grow emersed. Unlike most stems we sell, there is no emersed form to transition from — what arrives is submersed growth and it must stay submersed.
  • If the whorls thin and the lower stem goes bare, the light is not reaching far enough down. Replant the healthy tops and discard the bare stems rather than waiting.

products.title: Bolbitis Heudelotii (African Water Fern)
products.body_html:
Want a fern with real texture? Bolbitis heudelotii grows finely divided, almost translucent dark green fronds with a hammered surface — nothing else in a planted tank looks like it. It attaches to wood and stone rather than rooting in substrate, and it thrives in the kind of current most plants dislike.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as Bare-root plants, or Potted plants
  • Bare-root plants | approx. 6 leaf, bare-root, loose rhizome
  • Potted plants | approx. 6 leaf plant potted with rockwool and plastic net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — African Water Fern, Congo Fern
  • Scientific name — Bolbitis heudelotii
  • Origin — Tropical West and Central Africa
  • Placement — Midground to background, on wood or stone
  • Mature height — 8–14 in
  • Growth rate — Slow

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium. Bright light means algae on slow-growing fronds
  • CO₂ — Not required. It speeds growth but changes nothing else
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Not required. Attaches to hardscape and feeds from the water column
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed in paludariums
  • Propagation — Rhizome division

Grower’s Notes

  • Never bury the rhizome. Tie it to wood or stone with cotton thread or fishing line, with the rhizome fully exposed. Skip glue: it kills the tissue it touches. Buried in substrate it rots, and this is the usual way Bolbitis is lost.
  • Give it flow. This is a rheophyte from fast-running African streams, and it does visibly better in current than in still water. Placing it in the outflow path is one of the few reliable ways to speed it up.
  • It is genuinely slow. Expect a month or more before the first new frond appears, and do not move it while it settles — Bolbitis resents relocation more than most epiphytes.
  • Cooler suits it. At the top of its range growth slows further and fronds are more prone to browning at the edges.
  • Divide by cutting the rhizome with a blade, leaving several fronds and some root on each section.

New to attaching plants? Read our guide on how to attach epiphyte plants to driftwood and rock.

products.title: Amazon Sword Mother Plant
products.body_html:
Want a centerpiece today rather than in a year? The Amazon Sword Mother Plant is a mature XL specimen — approx. 10-12 inches on arrival — that reads as a background plant from the day it goes in, then keeps climbing. Swords are slow, so buying one already grown is the only way to skip the wait.

What You’ll Receive

  • Sold as a mother XL size, approx. 10-12 inches in height
  • Bare-root plants | Approx. 1-2 loose plants with root
  • Bunched plants | Approx. 1-2 plants with root, bundled with foam, and lead weight
  • Potted plants | Approx. 1-2 plants with root, potted with net pot and Rockwool

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Amazon Sword
  • Scientific name — Echinodorus bleheri
  • Also known as — Echinodorus grisebachii 'Bleherae'
  • Placement — Background or centerpiece
  • Shipped size — Approx. 10-12 in
  • Mature height — 16–24 in
  • Suits — 29 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Beginner
  • Light — Medium
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.5–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Heavy root feeder — root tabs are essential in inert gravel
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Plantlets on aerial floral stalks

Grower’s Notes

  • Give it a tank with real depth. A plant this size in a shallow aquarium grows into the lid, bends over and shades everything around it. 29 gallons is a sensible minimum.
  • Plant the crown at the substrate line, never below it. A buried crown rots, and that is how most newly planted swords are lost.
  • Root tabs are not optional. Swords feed almost entirely through their roots, and liquid fertilizer does very little for them. Small pale new leaves means root nutrition, nine times out of ten.
  • It propagates from aerial stalks, not runners. A mature sword sends a floral stalk upward or arching across the tank, carrying plantlets along its length. Let each plantlet develop three or four leaves and visible roots, then cut it free and plant it — a mother plant this size will produce them.
  • Expect the emersed leaves to melt back over two to four weeks while it converts. The submersed leaves that replace them are longer and thinner. Leave it alone through that.

products.title: Rotala Wallichii
products.body_html:
The finest-textured red stem in the hobby. Rotala wallichii grows needle-thin leaves in dense whorls, so a healthy group reads as a soft pink cloud rather than a set of stems. It is also one of the least forgiving — it wants high light, CO₂ and iron, and it tells you immediately when any of the three slips.

What You’ll Receive

Sold as loose fresh-cut plants, bunched plants, or potted plants:

  • Fresh-cut Plants: Approx. 6 individual, loose stems without roots
  • Bunched Plants: Approx. 6 stems without roots, bundled with foam and a lead weight
  • Potted Plants: Approx. 6 stems without roots, potted in rockwool and 2-inch net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Rotala Wallichii
  • Scientific name — Rotala wallichii
  • Also known as — Whorly Rotala, Mayaca-leaf Rotala
  • Origin — Southeast Asia
  • Placement — Midground to background, in dense groups
  • Shipped size — Approx. 6 fresh-cut stems, roughly 4-8 in
  • Mature height — 8–16 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Advanced
  • Light — High. Non-negotiable for both color and form
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 72–82°F · pH 6.0–7.0. Prefers soft, acidic water
  • Substrate — Required. Nutrient substrate or root tabs
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Cuttings — trim and replant stem tops

Grower’s Notes

  • Iron is what turns it pink. Light and CO₂ get you healthy growth; a dedicated iron-rich micronutrient dose is what produces the color this plant is bought for. Without it, expect a fine green plant.
  • Plant a dozen stems, not three. Wallichii looks thin and weedy as individual stems and only works as a mass — that's why the format sells in sixes and why buying two portions is usually the right call.
  • It sheds lower leaves fast in shade. Trim the tops, replant them, discard the bare stumps rather than waiting for regrowth.
  • It reacts to instability before other plants do. If wallichii starts dropping leaves, check CO₂ consistency before anything else — it works as an early warning for the whole tank.
  • Arriving green is normal. Color develops over several weeks under your lighting, not in the shipping box.

  • Rotala wallichii may arrive green when shipped, as coloration depends on lighting, nutrients, and CO₂. With the right care — including iron dosing, high lighting, and CO₂ injection — the plant will quickly develop its signature pink and red tones.

products.title: Micranthemum Monte Carlo Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
The forgiving carpet plant. Round bright-green leaves on creeping stems that form a dense lawn — easier to establish than HC Cuba, and it roots far more securely. Grown in sterile Vitro Culture®, so it arrives free of snails and algae.

  • Scientific name — Micranthemum tweediei 'Monte Carlo'

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high. Stronger light keeps it flat rather than climbing
  • CO₂ — Recommended, not required
  • Water — 68–78°F · pH 6.0–7.5
  • Substrate — Required. Fine nutrient substrate holds the plantlets best
  • Growth habit — Amphibious. Also grows emersed
  • Propagation — Runners — trim and replant

Grower’s Notes

  • It roots far more securely than HC Cuba. That is the main reason to choose it — newly planted portions stay put instead of floating off, which is the failure mode that defeats most first carpets.
  • Separate the culture into small portions and plant them an inch apart. It fills the gaps by runner faster than you expect.
  • Without CO₂ it still carpets, just slower and slightly taller. This is the carpet that works in a low-tech tank.
  • Trim once it reaches an inch. An untrimmed mat thickens, shades its own base, and starts lifting away from the substrate in sheets.
  • Rinse the gel off completely before planting. Also available as fresh-cut and potted plants.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Monte Carlo Care Guide.

Notes

  • Photos are for reference; color and density vary with lighting, CO₂ and nutrients.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Hygrophila Pinnatifida 'UK' Vitro Culture
products.body_html:
The redder pinnatifida. Hygrophila pinnatifida 'UK' — short for Uttara Kannada, the district in Karnataka it was collected from — carries more deeply lobed leaves and a stronger pull towards red than the common Goa form. Same creeping, hardscape-attaching habit; more color. This is the sterile Vitro Culture® format.

What You'll Receive

  • 1 sealed Vitro Culture® bag (4 inch) containing approx. 3-4 healthy young plants in liquid/gel agar.

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Pinnatifida 'UK'
  • Scientific name — Hygrophila pinnatifida 'Uttara Kannada'
  • Also known as — Hygrophila pinnatifida UK, Red Pinnatifida
  • Origin — Uttara Kannada, Karnataka, in the Western Ghats of India
  • Placement — Midground; attaches to driftwood and stone
  • Shipped size — Approx. 3-4 tissue-cultured plantlets, roughly 1-2 in
  • Mature height — 4–10 in
  • Suits — 10 gallons and up
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Low to medium. It grows in low light; the red needs stronger light
  • CO₂ — Recommended for best color and compact form
  • Water — 68–82°F · pH 6.0–7.5, soft to moderately hard
  • Substrate — Not required if attached to hardscape; nutrient substrate if planted
  • Growth habit — Rheophyte. Creeping and branching; roots onto wood and stone
  • Propagation — Cuttings — stem cuttings and lateral shoots

Grower's Notes

  • 'UK' is the one to buy for color. The widely sold Goa form runs olive to bronze; this collection reddens more readily under the same conditions. If you have grown standard pinnatifida and wanted more red from it, this is the answer rather than more light.
  • Pinholes in older leaves mean potassium. Pinnatifida shows a potassium shortfall before anything else in the tank does. Dosing clears it within a few weeks — it is not a pest or a disease.
  • Tie it to wood rather than burying it. Attached, it roots into the surface and creeps outward, which is the habit worth having. Buried deep in substrate the lower stem rots.
  • Trimming decides the shape — left alone it runs horizontally, topped repeatedly it bushes upward.
  • Separate the plantlets and rinse the gel off completely before attaching, or it feeds algae in the first weeks.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Hygrophila Pinnatifida Care Guide.

Notes

  • Colors and appearance may vary based on tank conditions. Tissue culture plants should be rinsed thoroughly to remove growing gel before planting. Photos shown are for reference and represent mature growth under ideal conditions.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.

products.title: Ludwigia Meta
products.body_html:
Ludwigia Meta is what people reach for when Ludwigia Pantanal has beaten them. It gives the same fine whorls of narrow leaves and the same orange-to-red burn under strong light, but without Pantanal's intolerance for anything less than perfect. Still uncommon in the trade, and still a centerpiece plant.

What You'll Receive

Choose the format that suits your aquascaping needs:

  • Fresh-Cut Plants: Approximately 6+ unrooted stems
  • Bunched Plants: 6+ fresh-cut stems without root, bundled with foam and plant weight
  • Potted Plants: 6+ fresh-cut stems potted in rockwool within a 2-inch net pot

Plant Profile

  • Common name — Ludwigia Meta
  • Scientific name — Ludwigia inclinata var. verticillata 'Meta'
  • Also known as — Ludwigia sp. 'Meta'
  • Origin — Departamento del Meta, central Colombia
  • Placement — Midground to background
  • Mature height — 6-14 inches
  • Growth rate — Medium

Care

  • Difficulty — Intermediate
  • Light — Medium to high
  • CO₂ — Recommended
  • Water — 68-82°F, pH 6.0-7.0. Soft water, carbonate hardness below 4°dH
  • Substrate — Nutrient-rich soil or root tabs, plus water column dosing
  • Growth habit — Amphibious stem, feeds from roots and water column
  • Propagation — Cuttings

Grower's Notes

  • It arrives green and it is supposed to. Our stock is grown emersed, where the leaves are plain green. Orange and red develop only after the plant converts to submersed growth under your lighting — usually three to four weeks in.
  • Soft water matters more than light. Meta colors and grows best with carbonate hardness under 4°dH. In hard water it stays green and slowly stalls no matter how much light and iron you throw at it — test KH rather than chasing a pH number.
  • Easier than Pantanal, same look. If you have lost Ludwigia Pantanal to melt or stunting, Meta gives a similar fine-leaved red without the same intolerance of imperfect conditions.
  • It branches poorly, so plant more stems. Meta grows straight up with little side-shooting. Density comes from planting a group close together, not from waiting for one stem to bush out.
  • Replant the tops, discard the bases. As with most fine-leaved Ludwigia, the lower stem goes bare with age. Cut the top few inches, replant them, and pull the old base.

Want to go deeper? Read our complete Ludwigia Care Guide.

Notes

  • Ludwigia Meta ships in its emersed green form. Once submerged and provided with strong light and nutrients, it will gradually develop its iconic orange to red hues. Slight leaf melt during transition is normal.
  • Never release aquarium plants into natural waterways.
